title: I am the gate (John 10:1–10)
hook: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man questioned three times, thrown out, and found again, and the word synagogue. Your line was one thing I know.

A sheepfold on a hillside: a rough circle of stone walls, chest high, with one gap for an opening. At night the sheep are led inside, safe from wolves and thieves. Jesus is still talking to the listeners who threw the healed man out. He tells them a picture-story: sheep, a gatekeeper, thieves who climb over the wall, and a shepherd who walks in through the door. John says plainly they didn't understand it. So Jesus tries again, more directly.

First, the shepherd. The sheep hear his voice, and "he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Not a herd. Names. Then the surprise: "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture." The King James says door; some modern Bibles say gate. Either way, it's the opening in the wall. John has given us I am sayings before: bread, light. Now, the way in. People often tell how a shepherd in that region might lie down across the gap at night, so nothing could get in or out without stepping over him. Whether or not every shepherd did that, it's a good picture of what Jesus is saying. And look at the words: go in and out. A gate isn't only for locking in. In, to rest at night. Out, to pasture in the morning. Then the verse behind today's line: "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly." The Greek word behind abundantly means more than enough, overflowing. Not just getting by. Life with something left over. Christians often hold this line as a picture of what faith is meant to be: not a smaller life fenced in by rules, but a bigger one, with a safe place to come home to.

Think of your day as it's going to go, how much of it is errands, emails, just getting through; that's real, and it's fine. Now picture one small thing that's more than necessary, a longer walk, a real conversation, cooking something properly, ten minutes outside, music you love played loud, and choose one. If you pray, give thanks for the life you have and ask for it in full; if not, just savor the thing you chose.
Sheepfold. The walled hillside pen Jesus pictures, with one gap for a gate: the shepherd leads his sheep in to rest, and out to pasture.
Your line: life to the full. In to rest, out to pasture. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians often quote John 10:10 when describing the life they hope faith brings.

chat.meaning: Jesus calls himself the door: in to rest, out to pasture. He came that they might have life, and have it more abundantly.

notes: Index title says 'gate'; KJV says 'door'. The script explains both.

The shepherd sleeping across the sheepfold's opening is a commonly told picture (from travelers' accounts of Middle Eastern shepherds); presented as 'people often tell' and 'whether or not every shepherd did'. Confirm.
Order of I am sayings: this script calls 'the door' the third (after bread 6:35 and light 8:12). Confirm consistency with day 620 (good shepherd as fourth).
John 10:6 says they did not understand; confirm.
